first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this because her uncle keeps offering to 'do the ceremony'. The opening tells me straight away that it's a short list fixed by law and names the four types. No fuss, no gushing. And it says the answer changes if they marry overseas, which is exactly the bit we haven't settled. I'll read on.

journey.quote: The person at the front of the ceremony is the one who makes it legal, so it pays to know which type yours is and how to check.
journey.reaction: Sensible. That's the practical point, and it's said plainly.

journey.quote: When the legal side is settled, Wedded Concierge can take on the celebration.
journey.reaction: Is Wedded Concierge a person or a department? Later it talks about a Wedded Advisor. I worked it out eventually, but it's two names for what I assume is one service.

journey.quote: A friend or family member can only legally marry you once registered as a celebrant, and assessment can take up to 6 months.
journey.reaction: There's my answer for my brother-in-law. Six months, and it isn't guaranteed. I'll forward that one.

journey.section: Who can legally perform a marriage in Australia?
journey.quote: You must not already be married, must not be marrying a close relative, must be at least 18 (unless a court has approved a marriage where one person is 16 to 18), must understand what marriage means and freely agree to it, and must use specific words during the ceremony.
journey.reaction: Everything here is fine, but it's one long sentence of 'must's. On the iPad I lost my place halfway through.

journey.quote: The two Commonwealth types share one regulator and one register, which is why they are sometimes grouped as a single type, with three groups in all.
journey.reaction: Four types, or three groups? I had to read it twice. I'd rather it just stuck with four.

journey.section: Can a friend or family member marry you?
journey.quote: Most couples keep it simpler. Book an authorised celebrant for the marriage itself, and ask your celebrant how a friend or family member can take part in the ceremony, whether through a reading, a welcome or a few words of their own.
journey.reaction: Good. That's the kind way to tell the family 'no' without anyone feeling left out. I can suggest he gives a reading.

journey.section: How to check your celebrant is authorised
journey.quote: Check before you pay a deposit. It takes a few minutes on the official register.
journey.reaction: Now we're talking. Anything that protects a deposit gets my attention, and the steps are numbered so I can follow them.

journey.section: How to check your celebrant is authorised
journey.quote: If something goes wrong, AGD also explains how to complain about a marriage celebrant.
journey.reaction: Someone accountable if it goes wrong. That reassures me.

journey.section: What your celebrant must do to make it legal
journey.quote: Plan the signing into the run sheet. If an error on a certificate is found after the ceremony, it can be corrected only while the couple and witnesses are still present.
journey.reaction: Practical, and the sort of thing nobody thinks of until it's too late. Sounds like people who've done this before.

journey.section: What your celebrant must do to make it legal
journey.quote: The celebrant keeps the celebrant copy of the official certificate for six years from the date of the marriage.
journey.reaction: This section gets a bit government handbook. I skimmed the certificate detail. It's the celebrant's job, not ours.

journey.section: Who can marry you if your wedding is overseas?
journey.quote: Not your Australian celebrant, at least not legally.
journey.reaction: Clear as day. I'd assumed they could bring someone from here. Glad I know now.

journey.section: Who can marry you if your wedding is overseas?
journey.quote: Your authorised celebrant marries you in Australia, with the NOIM lodged at least 1 month ahead, and the celebration overseas carries no legal weight of its own.
journey.reaction: This is the route I'd lean towards. Do the legal part here, where my mother can come without a long flight, then the celebration abroad.

journey.section: Who can marry you if your wedding is overseas?
journey.quote: If you marry abroad, check whether your paperwork needs an apostille, and read about registering an overseas marriage at home.
journey.reaction: Then four links in one paragraph: apostilles, registering at home, Smartraveller, celebrants abroad. It feels like being handed a pile of brochures and told to sort it out. If they choose the overseas legal route, who helps them through that?

journey.section: Who can marry you if your wedding is overseas?
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments for the celebration abroad as your single point of contact, in your time zone and quoting in AUD, while the legal ceremony stays with you and your celebrant: speak with Wedded Concierge.
journey.reaction: One person, our time zone, Australian dollars. And they're honest that the legal bit isn't theirs. I'd rather that than someone claiming to do everything.

journey.quote: Only if they are also an authorised marriage celebrant.
journey.reaction: The JP question. My brother-in-law is a JP and was sure that covered it. It doesn't. Very useful.

journey.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, anywhere in the world, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Fee in writing before any work begins. That's the line my husband will want to see.

unanswered_questions: If the kids do the legal ceremony here first, will the Wedded Advisor plan the overseas celebration around that date?
If they decide to marry legally abroad, who arranges the person who marries them over there, and does the Wedded Advisor keep an eye on that paperwork timeline or is it all on my daughter?
Is the first step a phone call with a real person before anything is booked or paid?

turn_offs_found.quote: You must not already be married, must not be marrying a close relative, must be at least 18 (unless a court has approved a marriage where one person is 16 to 18), must understand what marriage means and freely agree to it, and must use specific words during the ceremony.
turn_offs_found.why: Five requirements and a bracket squeezed into one sentence. On the iPad it's a block of text. Short bullet points would be far easier to read and to print for my husband.

turn_offs_found.quote: If you marry abroad, check whether your paperwork needs an apostille, and read about registering an overseas marriage at home.
turn_offs_found.why: The overseas section is the one we most need, and it ends in a paragraph that's mostly links. It reads like homework rather than an explanation, and it doesn't say who helps with any of it.

would_share_with: My brother-in-law, with 'Only if they are also an authorised marriage celebrant.' and the reading or welcome suggestion
My husband, with 'Check before you pay a deposit.' and the Wedded Advisor paragraph (AUD, fee agreed in writing)
My daughter, with the 'Marry legally at home, celebrate abroad' option

cta_reaction.quote: Start the conversation with Wedded Concierge.
cta_reaction.why: The paragraph before it says the right things: one Advisor, fee in writing before any work begins. But this article is about who marries them, and they haven't chosen the legal route yet. Once that's settled I'd click, and I'd want a phone call with a real person first.

top_3_changes: Turn the eligibility sentence ('You must not already be married, must not be marrying a close relative...') into a short bulleted list so it's readable on a tablet and easy to print.

Break the overseas link paragraph ('If you marry abroad, check whether your paperwork needs an apostille...') into a short 'if you marry abroad, check these' list, with a plain-words line on what each link is for.
Use one name consistently, or say in a few words that Wedded Concierge is how you reach your Wedded Advisor, and add one line on how the Advisor fits the celebration around the legal ceremony date.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Margaret (mother of the bride, paying about half, sent the link by her daughter, reads top to bottom on an iPad)
No invented brand facts; missing details listed as unanswered questions
HTML comments, image slots and VERIFY markers treated as invisible
Deferred business details (deposits, contracts, 2am contact) and transfers not raised as must-fix; absent prices, celebrant names and sourcing not raised as problems, per orchestrator
Journey types limited to the allowed enum; every turn-off has a why

open_questions.question: Main gaps for this persona: the dense eligibility sentence and the link-heavy overseas paragraph (readability); a mild Wedded Concierge vs Wedded Advisor naming confusion; and a parent wants one line on how the Advisor coordinates the celebration with the legal ceremony date. Relevance is naturally moderate as this is a couple's legal topic. Call-first is a deferred business detail.

assumptions: Margaret's daughter is the bride and sent the link because a relative (a JP) offered to marry them; the couple has not yet chosen between marrying legally in Australia or abroad. Margaret reads the whole article on an iPad.
Prices and celebrant names are deliberately absent and the brand does not discuss sourcing, so none were raised.
